title: ChatGPT as an automated writing evaluation (AWE) tool: feedback literacy development and AWE tools’ integration framework
extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI and other automated writing evaluation (AWE) tools can support learners’ feedback literacy in writing. The study is motivated by growing interest in ChatGPT for language learning, especially its possible role as a writing assistant and feedback provider, alongside established tools such as Grammarly and Quillbot. The core research question asks to what extent these AWE tools support the development of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students’ feedback literacy.

The intervention was the integration of ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Quillbot into a writing course. Students were introduced to self-evaluation using these tools, shown how ChatGPT could proofread, provide feedback, and paraphrase, and given a modeled prompt tied to the course writing rubric: “Revise my recount text and show the revision in terms of content, organization, grammar, vocabulary, and mechanics.” Students then used any AWE tool of their choice on draft essays in Google Docs e-portfolios, sometimes combining AI feedback with peer feedback, teacher feedback, Google searches, and word processor spell/grammar checkers. The study also develops an “AWE Tools Integration Framework” based on qualitative analysis of student experiences.

The population was 18 second-semester undergraduate English Education students at a private university in Surabaya, Indonesia, enrolled in a compulsory Recount and Narrative Essays course. The course lasted 16 weeks overall, with the focal data collection concentrated in the first seven meetings and approximately four months of study context described. Data came from semi-structured interviews with 12 volunteers, reflective journals, and student artifacts such as e-portfolios and feedback evidence. The setting was primarily classroom-based instruction with online drafting in Google Docs and LMS submission.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Quillbot, used alone or in combination, supported almost all aspects of students’ feedback literacy, but their usefulness varied by student proficiency, motivation, and ability to process automated feedback. ChatGPT was especially valued for generative functions such as paraphrasing, idea development, vocabulary enhancement, and style revision, while Grammarly and Quillbot were preferred for explicit grammar correction. At the same time, students reported limitations including confusion, over-reliance, ethical concerns, and uneven digital literacy. The authors argue that teachers should scaffold students’ use of AWE tools, support critical evaluation of AI output, and consider learner preference, tool features, technical capability, learning affordances, perceived limitations, and personal issues when integrating AI into writing instruction.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative single-case study with clear methods, data sources, and analytic procedures, but it is small, non-K-12, non-experimental, and lacks quantitative outcome estimation. It meets limited credibility criteria and therefore fits yellow rather than green or blue.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest potentially beneficial but highly mixed and context-dependent impacts, with no causal design or effect sizes and substantial heterogeneity by student proficiency/motivation. Overall impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrably positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Quillbot were used as automated writing evaluation tools for EFL essay drafting and revision, including grammar checking, paraphrasing, lexical enhancement, proofreading, and feedback on recount/narrative essays.

ChatGPT was specifically used conversationally to review student writing via prompts, generate revisions/feedback across rubric dimensions, paraphrase text, and support students' self-evaluation of essays.
The paper examines AI-enabled automated feedback on student writing, with students using tool-generated comments/corrections during drafting and revision as part of a feedback-literacy intervention.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative case study of 18 Indonesian undergraduate EFL students, ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Quillbot were perceived to support writing revision through grammar correction, paraphrasing, vocabulary enhancement, punctuation, and idea development, but students also reported inaccuracies, over-paraphrasing, text shortening, confusing corrections, and risk of uncritical uptake. Benefits appeared stronger for more proficient and motivated students, while lower-proficiency or less motivated students more often found the tools confusing or unhelpful. No standardized writing effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative evidence from semi-structured interviews, reflective journals, e-portfolio drafts, screenshots of tool use, and feedback artifacts about writing revision and self-evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The primary studied outcome was feedback literacy, with qualitative evidence suggesting the AWE tools supported multiple components such as appreciating feedback, eliciting feedback, and enacting feedback, while 'feedback processing' could be either enhanced or undermined depending on student behavior. Students who iteratively refined prompts, regenerated outputs, compared versions, and cross-checked suggestions showed stronger evaluative judgment and self-regulatory use; others reported overreliance, confusion, or blind acceptance of AI outputs. No quantitative scale scores or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative indicators of feedback literacy from interviews, journals, and writing artifacts, coded against Molloy et al.'s feedback literacy framework

finding.finding_summary: Students reported both positive and negative affective responses to AI-supported writing feedback: some valued the perceived objectivity and helpfulness of AWE tools, while others felt uneasy, considered ChatGPT use 'cheating,' worried about dependency, or found chatbot interaction strange. The paper also notes that Quillbot was perceived by some students as reducing anxiety, but these affective results were not systematically quantified in this study. No effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported attitudes, emotions, and perceptions in interviews and reflective journals

finding.finding_summary: Participants described AWE tools as making assignment completion and revision easier through rapid grammar checking, proofreading, paraphrasing, and immediate corrective suggestions. The discussion also notes potential workload relief for teachers by shifting surface-level editing to AWE tools, though this was discussed conceptually rather than directly measured. No time-on-task or productivity effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceptions of ease, speed, and convenience of revision; conceptual discussion of teacher workload relief
